# The black punk pioneers who made music history

## The rebel icons who defied cultural stereotypes to kickstart a musical revolution

November 
19, 
2015November 
19, 
2015Text
Daisy Jones



The meaning of ‘punk’ is hard to define. Is it an attitude? A genre? A willingness not to conform? Despite such ambiguities, punk is streotypically portrayed as the preserve of white, working-class musicians. Although as Charlie Brinkhurst-Cuff pointed out last week, “Punk music is not the sole property of whiteness, even though to people of my generation it may appear that way at first glance,” adding, “Like many facets of pop culture, its historical image has been whitewashed.” To celebrate the true punk rebellion that has always existed in black culture, and continues to exist today, here are just a few punk pioneers that changed the game and made their mark.

#### POLY STYRENE

Although 1970s punk band X-Ray Spex were self-confessed underachievers and only managed to release one album, the oddball five-piece created a beautifully discordant soundtrack to teen rebellion that remains relevant today. Spearheading their distinctive sound was Poly Styrene, one of the most effervescent and influential artists to emerge from the punk movement. “I just want to be like me,” she told _NME_ at the time. “I said that I wasn’t a sex symbol, and that if anybody tried to make one I’d shave my head tomorrow.”





#### DON LETTS

You can’t talk about pioneering figures in punk without mentioning Don Letts, the creative polymath and subcultural icon often credited with injecting the bouncing sounds of Jamaican reggae into the London punk scene. From spinning reggae records during punk nights at the Roxy, to managing The Slits and starting his own band (The Electric Dread), Letts passed his musical obsessions on to a generation hungry for change. “Don will always be an influential figure for youth culture in Britain because he channels his experiences and history,” designer Nicholas Daley told us earlier this year. “And he continues to collaborate with a variety of people and is always willing to work with creatives.”





#### PURE HELL

Pure Hell, the leather-clad, tatted-up, brooding four-piece, are often cited as one of the first all African American punk bands, and when they burst on to the scene from Pennsylvania to NYC in 1974, they found kindred spirits in the New York Dolls. “The Dolls took to us right away,” they commented. “We tended to remind them of themselves when they were younger. Part hoodlums, part musicians, the same mould.” Weirdly, their first album _Noise Addiction_ was released over 30 years later – but better late than never.





#### BAD BRAINS

Hardcore punks Bad Brains might have been flung out of Washington in 1977, but they sound like any given band you might find these days in some sweaty, cramped basement hangout. Although obviously – they came first. With their lightning-quick drumbeats, intense guitar riffs and lacerating vocals, Bad Brains pushed sonic boundaries and redefined people’s perceptions of what a group of Rastafarians were like in the 1970s. “I don’t care what people listen to, really,” the band’s bassist Darryl Jenifer once commented. “And I don’t care if black people ever get Bad Brains; that’s not on me. All I got to do is stay inventive and keep doing what I’m doing.”





#### DEATH

Long before The Clash, the Sex Pistols or the Ramones came Death, a proto-punk band from Detroit made up of three young black brothers, who started off as a soul band but quickly ditched that sound once they heard the hard, discordant rhythms of The Stooges. As Peter Margasak wrote in the _Chicago Reader_, their guitarist “pushed the group in a hard-rock direction that presaged punk, and while this certainly didn’t help them find a following in the mid-70s, today it makes them look like visionaries.” Their music has since been documented in the 2012 documentary _A Band Called Death_, a film that has won them a cult following decades after they disbanded.





#### MYKKI BLANCO

As an artist who’s emerged in the past five years, Mykki Blanco might seem like an anomaly on this list, but the pioneering punk spirit of NYC’s fearless riot-grrrl rapper shouldn’t be downplayed. With a subversive attitude to gender, genre and artistic medium, Blanco has redefined what it means to be punk in the present day. “I chose the name Mykki Blanco as an homage to Lil’ Kim’s persona Kimmy Blanco and also because I loved the name DeeDee Ramone – a feminine name on a punk rock singer,” she told us in 2012. “I did not grow up rapping; I grew up in the riot-grrrl queercore scene.”

articles.title: African Design — Deep Dive
articles.author: Anna Sansom
articles.summary: From Kossi Aguessy's retrospective at Togo's Palais de Lomé to Jean Servais Somian's coconut-palm furniture and Cheick Diallo's 30-year mission out of Bamako — a wide-angle look at contemporary African design's rise, its shared reuse-and-reinvent ethos, and the galleries (Cécile Fakhoury, 50 Golborne, Southern Guild) and fairs (AKAA, Collect, Beirut) making the market.
articles.body:
THE PALAIS DE LOMÉ, a new cultural venue in Togo, was inaugurated in December with an exhibition paying tribute to Kossi Aguessy, the visionary artist/designer of Togolese descent. In the renovated waterfront palace — constructed in 1905 and formerly serving as the German, then French, governors' residence — a diversity of Aguessy's pieces are on display. 'Kossi Aguessy: Infinity (1977-2017)' subtly blends African influences and Western production methods, from industrial design to sculptures and paintings, positioning him as a reference for Togo's upcoming generation at a moment when contemporary African design generally is garnering increased attention globally.

Born in Togo as Kossigan Baaba-Thundé Hervé Aguessy, he studied industrial and interior design at Central St Martins in London, worked for Philippe Starck, then set up his own Parisian studio in 2008. His 'Jord' chair (2012, layered oak) and 'Fogo' lamp (2012, organic LEDs at the tips of its branches) are in the Centre Pompidou's collection. When Sonia Lawson, director of the Palais de Lomé, conceived the idea for a design gallery, she thought of involving Aguessy in some capacity. News of his untimely death on his fortieth birthday — after battling cancer — prompted her to invite curator Sandra Agbessi to assemble a show celebrating his multi-faceted work.

The exhibition is named after Aguessy's scarlet 'Infinity' chair (2016), made from looping aluminium into a deformed figure of eight — lower part base, upper part seat. What emerges is his sculptural and technical wizardry: bronze honeycomb fruit bowls (2008-2010); the sumptuous 'Fjord' armchair in Carrara marble (2010); 'The Stool' (2014-2016), a brass stool of graceful simplicity; and smooth ceramic masks (2010-2016) reinterpreting traditional African masks. Endlessly curious about processes, Aguessy covered his stainless-steel prismatic totemic chair 'Useless Tool' (2008) with a low-reflective material used in aviation.

Earlier this year in Dakar, meanwhile, **Galerie Cécile Fakhoury** juxtaposed the work of Jean Servais Somian — who divides his time between Ivory Coast and Paris — and French artist Ana Zulma. 'Babitopie (Entre-Deux)' showed Somian's furniture carved from the trunks of coconut palms alongside photographs of Abidjan locals taken by Somian, painted over by Zulma. Among the pieces: stools and consoles embellished with wooden beads, and mirror-encrusted totems with holes carved into them where books and magazines can be inserted.

Somian, 48, studied cabinet-making with Georges Ghandour in Grand-Bassam and worked in Paris and Switzerland before exhibiting at the 2002 International Design Biennale of St-Etienne. He then established production in Ivory Coast in collaboration with local craftsmen. "When I discovered the coconut palm, whose wood is usually used to warm a hearth, I found it strange and beautiful to work with," he says. "I wanted to impose my signature so it could become an object at the crossroads of sculpture and design. It's the most magnificent plant: we can thatch roofs with its leaves, eat and make cosmetic products with its fruit, and make furniture from its trunk."

Somian buys coconut palms from landowners planning to cut them down: "When the landowners decide to build a house, they call and ask me if I want to buy the trunks and I choose the ones that interest me. Now they know that I want to buy them, they no longer throw them away." His 'Wooden Coconut Mobile Bar' — an oblong bar on wheels loosely inspired by a doctor's briefcase — won the best object award at Beirut Design Fair in September. In Grand-Bassam the bark is removed, wood carved and sculpted, forms take shape; then the pieces travel to his Abidjan atelier for finishings — drawers on cabinets, legs on consoles, bits of ox bone applied to the wood.

Somian also reconfigures the discarded canoes of Ivorian fishermen into sofas by adding fabric onto the empty inner structure and legs onto the base: "It saddens me when old and tired fishermen leave their canoes at the water's edge and they become rotten. As a designer, I want to find a solution and bring something magical to them." Feeling affinity with Senegal's Bibi Seck and Burkina Faso's Hamed Ouattara, he sees a shared philosophy across African designers: "By using locally sourced or recycled materials, we're transmitting a message: that one needs to look at what's happening close-by and facilitate the livelihood of the local community. In Africa, we don't have big manufacturing machines but that doesn't mean we can't create with what we have."

Styles vary — partly due to different tribal influences — but reinterpreting traditional craftsmanship and recycling materials are commonalities of design made in Africa. The Senegalese designers **Baay Xaaly Sene (BXS)** and **Ousmane Mbaye** have both ingeniously created furniture from old petrol barrels. A parallel trend: interest in African design filtering into the mainstream — as with IKEA's Överallt collection, made by ten African designers including Issa Diabaté, Selly Raby Kane, Bethan Rayner and Naeem Biviji.

Taking a different tack, Ethiopian-American industrial designer **Jomo Tariku** gleans ideas from the continent to define a new language of contemporary furniture. His 'Birth Chair II' (2016) — blackened wood with white motifs painted on the backrest — was born from deconstructing traditional Sub-Saharan African birthing chairs that support pregnant women during childbirth.

An early pioneer of African contemporary design is Mali's **Cheick Diallo**, whose furniture was included in the seminal 'Africa Remix' exhibition at the Hayward Gallery and the Centre Pompidou in 2004. His work is in the Musée des Arts Décoratifs, Paris, and was exhibited by Bamako Art Gallery at Also Known As Africa (AKAA) in November. After studying architecture and design in France, Diallo lived in Rouen and travelled to Bamako to collaborate with local craftspeople; he returned to Bamako six years ago. "I wanted to show that it's possible to make design in Mali," he said in 2017. "My philosophy was to develop manual, artisanal savoir-faire — because industry doesn't exist over here — and make contemporary, luxury objects with our own hands without importing things from abroad. People didn't believe me when I said my objects were made here."

Diallo works with weavers on meticulously woven and braided furniture and lighting, sometimes revealing Western sensibilities informed by Frank Gehry, Ron Arad and Constance Guisset; other pieces use recycled metal on a large metalworking site. "Africa needs to show that it can propose design projects to the whole world — that's the ambition and now it's happening on a bigger scale," says Diallo, who was commissioned to make furniture for the French and Belgian embassies in Bamako. Regarded as the "grandfather of African design", he co-founded and presided over the Association of African Designers, and organises workshops for young designers in Ivory Coast, Senegal, Ghana, Morocco and Tunisia.

"Cheick Diallo introduced the idea of reinventing local savoir-faire in Africa in the 1990s with an intellectual, conceptual and rigorous approach," says Pascale Revert, founder of **50 Golborne** in London. Revert discovered Diallo's work fifteen years ago through her first gallery, Perimeter Art & Design in Paris. Alongside Cape Town's **Southern Guild**, she is one of a small set of collectible-African-design dealers. At London's Collect fair she presented Uganda's Sanaa Gateja (mural beadworks), Nigerian ceramicist Ranti Bam, and Senegalese furniture designer Balla Niang.

The market for contemporary African design is led by European and American clients, but both Fakhoury and Revert believe the number of local collectors is growing. "Some live abroad, others have returned to their country of origin and have purchasing power," Fakhoury says. "The local African bourgeoisie is becoming interested in unique pieces in galleries in Abidjan, Lagos, Johannesburg, Cape Town and internationally," Revert concedes. "But economic structures are needed for significant market development. One hopes that 'starchitects' of African origin — such as David Adjaye and Francis Kéré, increasingly involved on the continent — will call on African designers for hotel, residential and social projects, like schools." Equally, venues like the Palais de Lomé are needed to stimulate a passion for design locally through exhibitions like the one on Aguessy.

articles.title: The rising stars of African design are championing heritage and craft
articles.author: Roddy Clarke
articles.summary: African design has long been overlooked internationally, but emerging designers are now gaining recognition for championing the continent's rich heritage of craft.
articles.body:
Stephen Tayo

# The rising stars of African design are championing heritage and craft

There’s a magnetism to African design that is long overdue acknowledgement on the global stage. But a shift is under way…

By Roddy ClarkePublished: 16 June 2024

African design has long been overlooked on the international stage, but recent years have seen the likes of Yinka Ilori, Amechi Mandi and Ozwald Boateng (whose collaboration with Poltrona Frau seems him pair thoroughly British furniture shapes with Ghanaian-inspired fabric) do much to champion the continent’s rich heritage of craft – a mantle that’s being picked up by these rising stars…

## Amwa Designs

Founded by British-Ghanaian multi-disciplinary designer and curator Chrissa Amuah, Amwa Designs is a London-based studio where the textiles, furniture and art draw inspiration from and pay homage to African design sensibilities.

Sophia SpringAmwa Designs’ founder Chrissa Amuah

Recent work includes the ‘Asanka’ table, which features, beneath its glass top, a jesmonite interpretation of a traditional asanka (a shallow clay bowl used in parts of West Africa to blend and grind food). Amuah says the table’s wooden base is inspired by the Ghanaian Adinkra symbol Adinkrahene (represented as a series of concentric circles), regarded as the most important of all the Adinkra symbols and linked to ideas of authority and leadership. With its off-centre silhouette, Amuah’s interpretation alludes to a combination of strength and vulnerability, and is available in multiple vibrant colour combinations. _amwadesigns.com_

## Altin Studio

Mehdi Kebaier and Yasmine Sfar founded this Tunisian studio to celebrate local design through the application of native materials. Working with sea rush, clay and palm wood, they create extraordinary artisanal pieces, bringing together their backgrounds of interior design (Sfar) and civil engineering (Kebaier), and referencing the traditional crafts of the country by interpreting age-old techniques through the viewpoint of contemporary design.

Bachir TayacAltin Studio founders Mehdi Kebaier and Yasmine Sfar

The studio’s ‘Ganymede’ cabinet, named after the largest natural satellite of the planet Jupiter, is a highlight. Its woven sea-rush panels provide contrast in colour and texture to the earth-red metal of the chequer-board design on top – the metal squares reference the pattern of the solar panels that unfurl around a satellite. Altin’s ‘Petite Ourse’ seat, hand-carved from palm wood, also alludes to the universe: the title translates as ‘Little Bear’, referencing the constellation of the same name._ altin.studio _

Altin Studio‘Petite Ourse’ seat by Altin StudioAltin Studio‘Ganymede’ cabinet by Altin Studio

## Nmbello Studio

Based in Lagos, Nigerian designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello says his design ethos is rooted in empathy and is connected to the continent through respect for people and places. With his humility prevalent in each project, the founder of Nmbello Studio has developed his body of work over the past decade while receiving several awards along the way – from the Hublot Design Prize in 2022 to the Curator’s Choice: Design for Good Award at Design Miami in 2023.

## What's everyone reading?

Stephen TayoNifemi Marcus-Bello founder of Nmbello Studio

‘Oríkì’, his most recent series, explores materiality and form with its first edition, ‘Act 1: Friction Ridge’, featuring a collection of bronze sculptural benches. Named after the practice of praise poetry among the Yoruba people of West Africa, the seats were launched in 2023 as part of an immersive installation that also featured a soundscape of the artist’s mother reciting his personalised oríkì. _nmbello.com_

## Mash.T Studio

Located in Johannesburg, Thabisa Mjo is the creative force behind Mash.T Studio. Producing furniture, lighting and homeware, she celebrates the rich cultural tapestry and traditions of South Africa through collaborations with communities of artisans, incorporating a variety of materials, from coloured beadwork (seen on her ‘Bright Light’ pendant) to repurposed telecommunication wire (used to create ‘Sprinkled Light’ and ‘4Kona Light’) – which is traditionally used by Zulu watchmen.

Lutendo MalatjMash T. Studio founder Thabisa Mjo

Recent lighting collections pay homage to the customs of the Xhosa people and the circular architectural forms found in rural areas across the country. Vibrant palettes also reference the season of summer, which, in Xhosa culture, signifies abundance and festivity. In celebrating the artistry that defines the cultural identity of the region, the studio allows local crafts and artisan communities to flourish and be recognised around the world. _mashtdesignstudio.com_

Mash T. Studio ‘4Kona Light’ by Mash T. Studio

## Rich Mnisi

Renowned for his sculptural and artistic flair, Johannesburg-born designer Rich Mnisi graduated from the LISOF School of Fashion in 2014 and won multiple awards before setting up his own fashion label. Mnisi also turned his hand to collectible furniture, bridging the gap between function and art.

Stephanie VeldmanJohannesburg-born designer Rich Mnisi

Taking inspiration from the women in his life, queerness and his heritage, his work has a striking fluidity and organic elegance. Most recently, his ‘Nwa-Mulamula’ chaise was on display in Los Angeles as part of Southern Guild’s ‘Mother Tongues’ exhibition, marking the opening of the Cape Town gallery’s new permanent space. The design references the shape of Mnisi’s great-grandmother’s reclining body. A similar affinity for sweeping silhouettes can be seen in new work ‘Vutlhari (Wisdom)’, a light crafted from bronze and resin. _southernguild.com_

Southern Guild‘Nwa-Mulamula’ chaise by Rich Mnisi at Southern Guild

## Xanthe Somers

This Zimbabwean artist draws inspiration from the customs of her homeland. Her hand-built ceramic sculptures, often functional in the form of lighting and vases (collection ‘In Bad Taste’), incorporate a range of materials and techniques, and continually challenge the political aspects of design and how it has been manipulated by colonialism in Zimbabwe. ‘I like to draw attention to Western overconsumption, cheap labour and the impact of eco-racist practices on the global south,’ she says.

Deniz GüselZimbabwean artist Xanthe Somers

‘I look at this in relation to patterns surrounding child- minding, caring, mending, fixing, stitching, cleaning, cultivating and crafting. My recent work looks to reimagine the everyday and examine the subtle treason of objects.’ Thanks to her vivacious use of colour, exaggerated silhouettes and thought-provoking narratives, the sculptor has had work displayed in London’s V&A Museum and at Somerset House’s Collect show. _xanthesomers.com_

## Don Tanani

Seeking to redefine the essence of Egyptian design while showcasing the country’s depth of talent, this contemporary brand is gaining a name for itself, thanks in part to a new collaboration with Lina Alorabi. The designer, who has had her work exhibited at the Milan Triennale and Nomad, moved back to her homeland of Egypt in 2009, after studying in the UK and gaining design experience in Germany.

Don TananiDon Tanani collaborator and designer Lina Alorabi

Over the past decade, she has immersed herself in the dynamism of Cairo, working alongside craft experts and visionary creatives. Her first collection for Don Tanani was launched in 2021 and her second, ‘Moruna’, landed recently. Oozing sophistication, it includes standout pieces such as a conversation chair, a curvaceous sun lounger and coffee tables with a tile pattern inset with glass. ‘The aim is to reclaim our identity, which is often translated to us from outside,’ says Alorabi. _dontanani.com_

Don Tanani

## Chuma Maweni

This South African ceramicist began his creative journey by crafting a series of vessels and conical pots using a pit-firing technique intrinsic to the artistic communities of the Nguni people. Maweni’s design aesthetic featured dark, porous surfaces alongside hand-formed sculptural outlines and decorative surface patterns, which raised his profile within the world of contemporary craft.

Micky HoyleSouth African ceramicist Chuma Maweni

Going on to open his own studio in Cape Town in 2016, the visionary talent has also showcased work on a global scale, exhibiting at shows such as Design Miami and The Salon Art + Design in New York. In addition, his work has been acquired by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. With his recent designs, such as the ‘Imbizo’ dining table and stools, being exhibited with Cape Town’s Southern Guild gallery, Maweni continues to celebrate traditional craft through a fresh perspective and contemporary lens. _southernguild.com _

articles.title: Oliver Wainwright obsesses over the distinctive architecture of Dakar
articles.author: Josh Niland
articles.summary: Léopold Sédar Senghor's call for a national style of 'asymmetrical parallelism' shaped a distinctive post-independence Senegalese modernism. Oliver Wainwright traces Dakar's 1970s–80s architecture — from the 1974 International Fair to the African Renaissance Monument — through the work of Cheikh Ngom, Pierre Goudiaby Atepa, and Henri Chomette.
articles.body:
Their obsessive geometrical composition was an attempt to answer the call of Senegal's first president, the poet Léopold Sédar Senghor, for a national style that he curiously termed "asymmetrical parallelism".

Senghor never quite defined what this brave new style should look like, but he spoke vaguely of "a diversified repetition of rhythm in time and space". Forceful, faceted forms and strong, rhythmic geometries became the vogue. — The Guardian

Dakar is known as a regional hub of modernism, which is equally the product of Senghor's arts-centered vision and of its past colonial linkage. Wainwright traced the history of post-independence architecture in Senegal from the 1974 International Fair to Abdoulaye Wade's controversial outsized African Renaissance Monument in Ouakam.

The Guardian critic appeared to be impressed by the city's variety of styles and influences, offering Philipp Meuser and Adil Dalbai's guide to the region as his bible and saying that it "offers a glimmer of hope from a new generation of young architects and engineers rediscovering vernacular techniques."

"It is the postcolonial architecture of the 1970s and 80s that really stands out for its originality, much of it by Senegalese architects Cheikh Ngom and Pierre Goudiaby Atepa, as well as France's Henri Chomette. They all developed a distinctive form of modernism in tune with President Senghor's ideas of asymmetrical parallelism. Monolithic tapering pillars, often in rough-textured concrete, support powerful chiselled volumes, with an inventive use of pebbles, rocks and shells to add a tactile, rugged texture to the almost primitivist forms."

articles.title: Griot in the Rubble: Boko Yout's Afro-Grunge as Diaspora Ritual
articles.author: ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial
articles.summary: Born of Togolese and Mozambican roots in the whiteness of provincial Sweden, Paul Adamah makes music that functions as riot and ritual — a genre-demolishing collision of ancestral memory, punk rebellion, vodún reclamation, and radical self-making.

embeds.why: Official video — GUSTO (title track, debut album 2025)

articles.body:
Paul Adamah was born in 1998 in Örebro, a mid-sized Swedish city that appears in statistical surveys and little else. His father came from Togo. His mother from Mozambique. In a city where Protestantism and whiteness shaped the ambient culture, Adamah learned early what diaspora children learn: how to shapeshift. How to shrink. How to translate yourself into whatever register a room demands.

It is from this quiet labour of self-erasure that Boko Yout was born.

**The Griot Tradition**

In West African culture, the griot is not merely a musician. The griot is a living archive — keeper of genealogy, political commentator, praise-singer and elegist. Their knowledge is preserved not in libraries but in the body, in the breath, in the performance. To be a griot is to be a node in a network that spans centuries, carrying what colonialism tried to silence in the one register that cannot be fully colonised: song.

Adamah named his 2024 collaborative EP _Griot_ without irony. The project, recorded with Stockholm-based producer boerd (Bård Ericson), fuses trip-hop electronics with raw vocal confessional — Ericson's lush, melodic textures holding space for Adamah's unflinching honesty. The EP arrived as both an exercise in cross-diaspora collaboration and a statement of method: this is music as ancestral conversation. The two met at a Way Out West gig, bonded over a shared reverence for British trip-hop's emotional directness, and retreated to build something intimate and strange. What emerged feels simultaneously ancient and immediate — as if the 1990s Portishead archives had been passed through a West African mouth and given new teeth.

**Afro-Grunge as Refusal**

Boko Yout's self-coined genre tag — Afro-Grunge — is not marketing. It is a refusal.

Grunge, as a form, was always about refusing polish. About breaking the guitar in ways that weren't fashionable. About using distortion not for stadium spectacle but to excavate discomfort. Boko Yout takes that same formal refusal and runs it through a different history — not the white working-class Pacific Northwest, but the Black European diaspora, the children of colonised nations navigating the metropoles of their former colonisers.

Afro-Grunge is what happens when the emotional rawness of punk meets the sonic memory of the African continent. It is what happens when a child of Togo and Mozambique picks up a distorted guitar in Sweden and refuses to make it sound like anything other than exactly what it is. The band — now a full four-piece with Joel Kiviaho, Kevin Stierne and guitarist Lionel Turner alongside Adamah — approaches guitar chaos with the mindset of a cinematographer: every sound a visual choice, every riff a narrative decision.

**GUSTO and the Therapy of Becoming**

The debut album _GUSTO_, released September 5, 2025, is framed as a series of therapy sessions. The fictional Dr. Gusto is the analyst. Adamah's alter ego Mordecai is the patient. The 13 tracks are the sessions — self-interrogation conducted at full volume, clocking in at just under 35 minutes.

This framing is not accidental. The language of therapy — interiority, excavation, the naming of what hurts — is a deeply political act for a Black artist navigating white cultural space. Frantz Fanon understood this when he wrote that the colonised subject internalises the coloniser's gaze until it becomes their own inner voice. The work of decolonisation is always also psychological: the work of distinguishing your own voice from the one that was installed in you.

_GUSTO_ performs this work noisily. The title track has been described as a collision between Queens of the Stone Age, Nine Inch Nails, and The Prodigy — but that description only captures the texture. The content is stranger and more specific: a man demanding the right to take up space, to expand, to be ungovernable in his own body and imagination. _9-2-5_ takes the grammar of the labour anthem and warps it into something more destabilising. _DEMOLITION MAN_ is exactly what it sounds like.

"I like the term joyful expansion," Adamah said in 2025. "Always acting out of your greatest desire or greatest joy. That's what I'm doing now."

**Vodún and the Reclamation of Fear**

Part of what makes Boko Yout's project distinctly post-colonial is its relationship to vodún — the spiritual tradition his Togolese father practiced. Adamah has spoken about fearing it as a child, shaped by the ambient Protestant culture of Örebro into suspicion of his own inheritance. That fear has given way to understanding and deliberate reclamation.

This is an old story, replayed in every diaspora: the child who grows into the parent's tradition after being taught to fear it. Colonialism's most effective tool was not the gun but the shame — the coding of African spiritual life as primitive, dangerous, backwards. The reclamation of vodún is therefore not merely spiritual. It is political. It is the refusal of that shame.

**The Body as Stage**

Live, Boko Yout is kinetic and generous. Adamah has described overcoming a deep fear of moving his body onstage — of taking up space physically. "I used to be scared to move a certain way," he has said. "As soon as I embraced that I was just me, this queer superstar, people started moshing and dancing naturally."

The body onstage is always political. For a Black queer artist performing in predominantly white European venues, to refuse to shrink — to mosh, to expand, to be ungovernable — is to enact the same politics that Boko Yout encodes in the music itself. It is the same politics the griot enacted, village to village, century to century: refusing to disappear.

**Griot, Again**

Boko Yout has received Newcomer of the Year nominations at the Swedish Grammis and Artist of the Future recognition at the P3 Guld Awards. These institutions are mainstream European music infrastructure — precisely the apparatus one might expect to misread what Boko Yout is doing.

And yet visibility matters. Not because institutions validate art, but because visibility creates lineage. It ensures that the next child of Togo and Mozambique growing up in Örebro or Gothenburg or Rotterdam will be able to point at something and say: this is possible. This is what it can look like. The griot's role is not only to preserve the past. It is to name what the future might become.

_GUSTO_ is, in the end, an album about exactly that: the possibility of becoming something you were told you couldn't be, in the exact register you were told to suppress.

Boko Yout is the noise that makes that possible.

articles.title: 7 Underrated African Heroes You Should Know About
articles.author: Jacqueline Traoré
articles.summary: Behind Mandela and Nkrumah stand generations of women, poets, prisoners, and organisers whose contributions were as decisive — and far less remembered. Seven pan-African figures worth learning by name.
articles.body:
Names like Nelson Mandela and Kwame Nkrumah dominate the popular story of African liberation. But behind them stand generations of women, poets, prisoners, and organisers whose contributions were as decisive — and far less remembered. This list, adapted from Jacqueline Traoré's original piece for Okayafrica, is a small correction.

**1. Josina Muthemba Machel (1945–1971)**

Mozambican independence leader who founded and led the Women's Detachment armed group within FRELIMO, one of the earliest gender-integrated liberation formations in colonial Africa.

**2. Ahmed Sékou Touré (1922–1984)**

Guinea's first president who in 1958 refused De Gaulle's terms and rejected French colonial authority outright — famously saying he preferred poverty in freedom to riches in slavery.

**3. Yaa Asantewaa (1840–1921)**

Ashanti queen-mother, politician, and military strategist who in 1900 led the Ashanti rebellion against British rule to defend the sacred Golden Stool.

**4. Sedick Isaacs**

South African anti-apartheid activist imprisoned on Robben Island who kept fellow prisoners' spirits alive through clandestinely organised sports and secular education.

**5. Es'kia Mphahlele (1919–2008)**

South African writer, essayist, and educator — the first Black professor at Witwatersrand University — who worked to institutionalise African literature as a serious field of study.

**6. Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (1900–1978)**

Nigerian anti-colonial activist and founder of the Abeokuta Women's Union whose organising against unjust taxation forced the abdication of the Alake of Egbaland in 1949.

**7. Mariama Bâ (1929–1981)**

Senegalese writer and activist whose novel _So Long a Letter_ became a landmark of African feminist literature, indicting polygamy, gendered inequality, and violence against women.

None of these figures acted alone. They belonged to movements, unions, courts, villages, prisons, and diasporas that shared the labour of freedom. To remember them is to remember that African liberation was never the work of a handful of men in suits — it was, and remains, collective work.

articles.title: Pan-African Heroes
articles.author: PANAUSUG
articles.summary: A working roll-call from the Pan-African Unity Summit Group — twelve figures across the continent and the diaspora whose lives argue that the freedom of one Black nation is bound up with the freedom of all.
articles.body:
The Pan-African Unity Summit Group (PANAUSUG) maintains a rolling list of figures across the continent and the diaspora whose lives argue, in different registers, that the freedom of one Black nation is bound up with the freedom of all. This is a selection.

**1. Martin Luther King Jr.**

American civil rights leader whose nonviolent strategy against Jim Crow became a template for freedom movements from Soweto to Selma.

**2. Nelson Mandela**

South African revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison, then walked out to negotiate the end of apartheid and became the country's first Black president.

**3. Kwame Nkrumah**

Ghanaian independence leader and architect of continental Pan-Africanism, who insisted Ghana's freedom was meaningless unless the whole of Africa was free.

**4. Patrice Lumumba**

Congolese nationalist and first prime minister of an independent Congo, assassinated within months for refusing to trade the country's sovereignty back to its former colonisers.

**5. Robert Sobukwe**

South African anti-apartheid thinker and founder of the Pan Africanist Congress, whose Sharpeville-era leadership landed him in prison under a law written just for him.

**6. Ella Baker**

American civil rights organiser who built the grassroots infrastructure of SNCC and insisted that strong people don't need strong leaders.

**7. Marcus Garvey**

Jamaican-born founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association, whose 'Africa for the Africans' organising put Pan-Africanism on ships and in newspapers on both sides of the Atlantic.

**8. Harriet Tubman**

American abolitionist and Underground Railroad conductor who liberated dozens from slavery and later served as a Union spy in the U.S. Civil War.

**9. W.E.B. Du Bois**

African American sociologist and Pan-Africanist theorist who convened the early Pan-African Congresses and argued Black identity across the diaspora was politically bound together.

**10. Winnie Madikizela-Mandela**

South African anti-apartheid activist and political leader whose defiance under police terror kept the movement alive during Nelson Mandela's decades in prison.

**11. Bob Marley**

Jamaican musician whose reggae carried a Pan-African, anti-colonial politics into pop culture worldwide — from Harare's independence stage to Trench Town.

**12. Anna Julia Cooper**

African American educator, writer, and feminist intellectual whose 1892 essays argued that Black women's freedom was the measure of any real liberation.

Pan-Africanism has never been about hero-worship. It's a working thesis — that our histories rhyme, our struggles overlap, and our victories should too. Each of these lives is a footnote to that thesis.

articles.title: 24 African Heroes Who Stood By Their Beliefs
articles.author: AfroBiz Africa (list) · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (bios)
articles.summary: Twenty-four figures whose lives turned on refusing to trade their beliefs for safety — from Mandela and Sankara to Amina of Zazzau, Njinga, Mansa Musa, Fela, and Chimamanda. A roll-call adapted from AfroBiz Africa.
articles.body:
AfroBiz Africa published a list of 24 figures whose lives — across the continent and the wider Black Atlantic — turned on refusing to trade their beliefs for safety. This is that roll-call, retold in a single register, with brief editorial notes.

**Nelson Mandela — South Africa, 1918–2013**

Anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years imprisoned for resisting racial rule, then led the peaceful transition to multiracial democracy and served as South Africa's first Black president.

**Wangari Maathai — Kenya, 1940–2011**

Environmentalist and organiser who founded the Green Belt Movement, planting tens of millions of trees while challenging state land grabs. First African woman awarded the Nobel Peace Prize (2004).

**Patrice Lumumba — DR Congo, 1925–1961**

Independence leader and first prime minister of Congo, assassinated within months of taking office for refusing to trade the country's sovereignty back to its former colonisers.

**Thomas Sankara — Burkina Faso, 1949–1987**

Revolutionary president who redistributed land, banned female genital cutting, mass-vaccinated the country, and refused foreign debt before being assassinated in 1987.

**Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie — Nigeria, 1977–**

Novelist and essayist whose fiction (_Half of a Yellow Sun_, _Americanah_) and 'We Should All Be Feminists' talk reset public conversation about African literature and gender.

**Kwame Nkrumah — Ghana, 1909–1972**

Led Ghana to independence in 1957 and became the continent's most articulate exponent of Pan-Africanism, insisting Ghana's freedom was meaningless without the freedom of all Africa.

**Yaa Asantewaa — Ghana, 1840–1921**

Ashanti queen-mother who in 1900 led the last major armed rebellion against British rule in the Gold Coast to defend the Golden Stool.

**Steve Biko — South Africa, 1946–1977**

Co-founder of the Black Consciousness Movement who argued psychological liberation had to precede political liberation. Beaten to death in police custody at 30.

**Miriam Makeba — South Africa, 1932–2008**

Singer and activist who used the world stage to expose apartheid, testified against it at the UN, and was stripped of her South African citizenship for it.

**Kofi Annan — Ghana, 1938–2018**

UN Secretary-General who advanced human-rights doctrine and the Responsibility to Protect; shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2001.

**Ellen Johnson Sirleaf — Liberia, 1938–**

Economist and first woman elected head of state in Africa, who led Liberia out of civil war and shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize.

**Haile Selassie — Ethiopia, 1892–1975**

Emperor who took Italy's 1935 invasion to the League of Nations with the speech that named collective security's price; later a founding figure of the OAU and spiritual reference-point for Rastafari.

**Frederick Douglass — United States, 1818–1895**

Formerly enslaved orator, writer, and abolitionist whose autobiographies and newspapers helped dismantle the moral case for slavery in the US.

**W.E.B. Du Bois — United States, 1868–1963**

Sociologist, NAACP co-founder, and Pan-Africanist theorist who convened the early Pan-African Congresses. Died in Ghana, a citizen of Nkrumah's republic.

**Amina of Zazzau — Nigeria, c.1533–c.1610**

16th-century Hausa warrior queen who expanded the city-state of Zazzau's territory and built the defensive walls still named for her.

**Mariama Bâ — Senegal, 1929–1981**

Senegalese writer whose epistolary novel _So Long a Letter_ became a foundational text of African feminist literature.

**Mansa Musa — Mali, c.1280–c.1337**

Emperor of the Mali Empire whose 1324 hajj through Cairo destabilised the region's gold price for a decade and put West African wealth on European maps.

**Desmond Tutu — South Africa, 1931–2021**

Anglican archbishop whose moral leadership under apartheid and chairing of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission won him the 1984 Nobel Peace Prize.

**Abdias do Nascimento — Brazil, 1914–2011**

Afro-Brazilian playwright, senator, and Pan-Africanist who theorised _quilombismo_ and founded the Black Experimental Theatre.

**Njinga Mbande (Queen Nzinga) — Ndongo & Matamba, 1583–1663**

17th-century queen who fought Portuguese slaving expeditions in what is now Angola for nearly four decades and negotiated as an equal with European powers.

**Chinua Achebe — Nigeria, 1930–2013**

Novelist whose _Things Fall Apart_ became the first African novel to enter the global literary canon on African terms, dismantling the colonial gaze from within.

**Thomas Mapfumo — Zimbabwe, 1945–**

Musician whose chimurenga music soundtracked the Zimbabwean liberation war and, later, his own exile for naming ZANU-PF's corruption.

**Marcus Garvey — Jamaica, 1887–1940**

Founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association whose 'Africa for the Africans' movement put Pan-Africanism onto ships and newspapers across the Black Atlantic.

**Fela Kuti — Nigeria, 1938–1997**

Afrobeat originator, band-leader, and self-described 'Chief Priest' whose music indicted military rule and the corruption it left behind.

A note on the source: AfroBiz's original page had content errors in its last eight entries (biographies duplicated from earlier names). The list of names is theirs; the individual bios above have been rewritten for accuracy while preserving the roll-call.

articles.title: An Unsung South African Hero: Cpl W. Cloete
articles.author: The Observation Post (SAMIL History)
articles.summary: Corporal William Cloete of the Cape Coloured Corps won the Military Medal for carrying ten wounded comrades out of German fire in the Italian campaign, then was blinded by a sniper at 24. He spent the rest of his life as a basket-maker in Bellville and died in 1993 — barely mentioned in South African military histories.
articles.body:
William Cloete was a Corporal in the Cape Coloured Corps, attached to the Cape Town Highlanders as leader of a stretcher-bearer team fighting the Italian campaign of the Second World War.

In one action his company was pinned down on three sides by German mortar and machine-gun fire. Under persistent enemy fire, Cloete and his team carried ten of their own wounded to safety. He was awarded the Military Medal for bravery.

Roughly a year later, at 24, he was hit by a German sniper's bullet and permanently blinded in both eyes.

After the war Cloete attended the School for the Blind in Bellville, became an expert basket-maker, and worked at that craft the rest of his life. He died in 1993.

South African military histories rarely mention him. On Armistice Day — 11 November — his fellow veterans still salute his name. This piece, from the SAMIL History Observation Post, is one of the few places online where his story is written down at length.

Cape Coloured Corps soldiers fought in every South African theatre of the Second World War and were, until the 1970s, buried under separate honours from their white comrades. Retrieving names like Cloete's is not a footnote to the story — it is the story.

articles.title: Jean-Pierre Bekolo: The Cameroonian Filmmaker Who Refused to Translate
articles.author: ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial
articles.summary: The Cameroonian director of Quartier Mozart, Les Saignantes, and Le Président has spent thirty years arguing that African cinema will not be free until African filmmakers stop trying to make films the West can love.
articles.body:
Jean-Pierre Bekolo does not make African films that translate for the West. He makes African films that argue with the West — and with African cinema itself — about what an African film is even for.

Born in Yaoundé in 1966, Bekolo studied physics at the University of Yaounde before switching to a form of storytelling that would let him keep asking physics-shaped questions: what are the laws of the world we live under, and who gets to rewrite them? He edited television in Cameroon, then trained at the Institut national de l'audiovisuel in France under the semiologist Christian Metz. He has been arguing back at the medium ever since.

**Quartier Mozart (1992)**

His first feature was a hand grenade. _Quartier Mozart_ opens with a schoolgirl who wants to know what men are really like; a witch grants her wish and turns her into a man for a day. What follows is a neighbourhood-scale folktale about desire, gender, and the swagger of Cameroonian street power, shot with the kinetic freedom of the French New Wave and the rhythmic sense of a music video. It won the Prince Claus Award, a special prize at Locarno, and a British Film Institute award — and announced a filmmaker for whom African cinema had never been a genre of pity or ethnography.

**Aristotle's Plot (1996)**

For the BBC's centenary-of-cinema project, Bekolo was asked to represent Africa. He answered with _Aristotle's Plot_, a film in which an African filmmaker named 'Cineaste' is tormented by a gang of movie-mad hoodlums whose taste runs to Schwarzenegger, Stallone, and Bruce Lee. The gang's leader is literally called 'Cinema.' It is a comedy about a real problem: the audience African filmmakers were told they were saving had already been colonised by Hollywood, and the Aristotelian three-act structure the industry insists on may not be their story's natural shape. The film premiered at Sundance and remains one of the sharpest pieces of film-criticism-as-film ever made from the continent.

**Les Saignantes (2005)**

Then he made science fiction. _Les Saignantes_ — 'The Bloodettes' — is set in Cameroon in 2025 and follows two young women who, after one of them accidentally kills a corrupt cabinet minister mid-coitus, methodically dismantle the country's entire political class. It is a martial-arts film, a horror film, and a mystical political manifesto rolled into one, drenched in high-contrast greens and blues and set to a pounding electro score. It won the Silver Yennenga at FESPACO and has been called by scholars one of the first African science-fiction features. Bekolo prefers a different framing: he calls it a warning.

**Le Président (2013)**

_The President_ imagines a Cameroonian head of state who has ruled for forty-two years and vanishes on the eve of another election. As the country panics, the film uses the missing president as an X-ray of the country's institutions, its media, its churches, and its citizens. It was banned in Cameroon before its release. Bekolo screened it anyway, sometimes in the open air.

**Naked Reality (2016) & the recent work**

His 2016 _Naked Reality_ is a black-and-white afrofuturist film set in a post-collapse Africa of 2065; its characters navigate a world where an ancient spiritual crisis has to be resolved before the ecological one can be. He has continued through the 2010s and 2020s with essay-films (_Africa, Thought in Motion_, on Dakar's schools of thought), political shorts (_Miraculous Weapons_, on freedom of expression), and installation work at SAVVY Contemporary in Berlin and the Musée du Quai Branly in Paris. He has taught at Virginia Tech, UNC-Chapel Hill, and Duke, where he refuses the traditional professor-student hierarchy in favour of what he calls 'Author Learning' — you learn to make films by making them, alongside someone who is currently making one.

**The argument he keeps making**

Bekolo returns, in almost every film and interview, to a single argument: African cinema will not be free until African filmmakers stop trying to make African films the West can love. That means abandoning the salvage-anthropology genre, refusing the humanitarian gaze, and — crucially — refusing the Aristotelian narrative machinery that assumes the West's sense of what a story is is the human sense of what a story is. His films look strange to Western critics because they were never trying to look like anything the West already knew.

Which is also why his best work — _Les Saignantes_, _Le Président_, _Aristotle's Plot_ — feels less like African cinema for export and more like something a lot of us on the continent, and in the diaspora, have been waiting a long time to see: an African filmmaker for whom the future is a genre he intends to claim.

articles.title: Sunny War, 'Anarchist Gospel' — Bandcamp Daily's Album of the Day
articles.author: John Morrison (review) · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Nashville guitarist Sydney Lyndella Ward — Sunny War — navigates a binary as old as Black American music itself, blending gospel with blues, country and rock n' roll. Bandcamp Daily's John Morrison called Anarchist Gospel a significant statement — proof that emotional, political and spiritual wholeness is still available if you're willing to work for it.
articles.body:
Sunny War — legal name Sydney Lyndella Ward — is a Nashville-based guitarist, singer and songwriter whose 2023 album _Anarchist Gospel_ engages a tension as old as Black American music itself: the working out of the sacred against the secular, the gospel against the blues, and what a Black artist owes to either.

The review, by John Morrison for Bandcamp Daily, traces how enslaved Africans smuggled a spiritual and musical inheritance into Christian worship and how the duality that came out of that smuggling — worship on Sunday, juke joint on Saturday night — has shaped Black music ever since. War, Morrison argues, is consciously working inside that duality and trying to move through it rather than pick a side.

Musically the record fuses gospel, blues, country and rock, held together by War's fingerpicked guitar and a vocal style that runs from whispered folk confession to church-raised power. 'Love's Death Bed' opens the record as a slow meditation on heartbreak; 'No Reason' rides a country-rock arrangement while its lyric turns on the incoherence of human beings; 'I Got No Fight' lands in a blues lineage — the specific exhaustion of navigating an anti-Black world, named without theatre.

War's cover of Dionne Farris's 'Hopeless' is picked out as a highlight, a demonstration of what her voice can carry when it isn't accompanying her own words. The guitar work through the record is understated on purpose — never virtuoso for its own sake, always in service of the song.

The reviewer's read is that _Anarchist Gospel_ is a significant statement: a record that reconciles emotional, political and spiritual contradictions in Black musical tradition without pretending they were ever really separate, and that suggests wholeness — cultural, personal, political — is still available if you're willing to work for it.

For a site cataloguing afro-anarchist sound-worlds, the album's title is more than gesture. War comes out of the LA punk / DIY scene; the anarchism in the name isn't decoration, it names a practice — the refusal of settled hierarchies whether they're church, industry, or genre.

articles.title: African Art: This Was Never Just a Mask
articles.author: Mr. E on Art History (video) · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: A 20-minute survey of African art history that refuses the tourist framing: from Nok terracottas and Ife bronzes to modern and contemporary African practice, the through-line is that masks were never 'just masks' — they were active political and spiritual instruments the West filed away as ethnographic curios.
articles.body:
Mr. E on Art History's twenty-minute survey lands one of the harder arguments in African art in one line: the mask was never just a mask.

The video introduces major themes across the continent's art history — from Nok terracottas and Ife bronzes through the artistic economies of the Mali, Benin and Kongo kingdoms, into the ruptures and adaptations forced by the transatlantic slave trade and formal colonisation, and forward into modern and contemporary African practice. The through-line is that African art has never been one style, one function, or one moment.

The maker's core methodological move is refusal — refusal of the older European framing in which African objects were 'primitive', 'tribal' or interesting mainly for their influence on Picasso. The masks the West filed away as ethnographic curios were, in their original context, active political and spiritual instruments: they made covenants, transferred authority, staged justice, made ancestors present.

The section on the colonial encounter treats African art as one of the terrains on which the colonial project was contested — objects were taken to European museums (many still there), traditional forms were repressed or rerouted through mission schools, and new hybrid practices emerged in the workshops and academies of the twentieth century. Modern and contemporary artists — the video points to figures across a continent-scale scene — have been recovering and remaking those inheritances on their own terms.

For a library concerned with afro-anarchism and contemporary African art this is a useful primer: watchable at a sitting, honest about its own generalist scope, and clear that treating African art as one thing is itself a legacy of empire.

articles.title: Thomas Sankara
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Thomas Isidore Noël Sankara was a Burkinabé military officer, Marxist and Pan-Africanist revolutionary who ruled as the first president of Burkina Faso from 1983 until his assassination in 1987. In four short years he tried to break his country loose from imperial debt, patriarchy and dependency, and became a lasting symbol of African self-determination.
